title: Zoetis (ZTS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript
transcript:
Competitive pressure eased in dermatology, but clinic visits softened

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Nov. 5, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

TAKEAWAYS

SUMMARY

Zoetis Inc.(ZTS-7.95%)reported that a diversified portfolio provided resilience as competitive pressures in the companion animal segment offset growth in livestock and diagnostics. Management narrowed full-year 2026 revenue guidance while raising expectations for adjusted diluted earnings per share, reflecting performance that met internal expectations despite macroeconomic headwinds. The company directed resources toward defending leadership positions in dermatology and parasiticides through targeted gross-to-net investments. While U.S. clinic visits declined, the livestock segment benefited from sustained demand for quality protein and productivity-enhancing biologicals in international markets.

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator:Welcome to the Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Conference Call and Webcast for Zoetis. Hosting the call today is Mathieu Aussermeier, Senior Vice President, Corporate Finance for Zoetis. Presentation materials and additional financial tables are currently posted on the Investor Relations section of zoetis.com. The presentation slides can be managed by you, the viewer, and will not be forward automatically. In addition, a replay of this call will be available approximately two hours after the conclusion of this call via dial-in or on the Investor Relations section of zoetis.com. At this time, all participants have been placed in a listen-only mode, and the floor will be open for your questions following the presentation. Instructions will be given at that time.

It is now my pleasure to turn the call over to Mathieu Aussermeier. You may begin.

Mathieu Aussermeier:Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Zoetis third quarter 2026 earnings call. I am joined today by Kristin Peck, Chief Executive Officer, and Jay Saccaro, Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operating Officer. This morning, we issued a press release announcing our third quarter 2026 financial results. Before we begin, I would like to remind you that the release and corresponding earnings presentation, which we will reference during this call, are available on the Investor Relations section of our website, and that many of our statements today may be considered forward-looking statements, and that actual results could differ materially from those projections.

For a list and description of certain factors that could cause results to differ, I refer you to the forward-looking statements in today's press release and in our company's Exchange Act reports filed with the SEC. Additionally, today's remarks will include certain non-GAAP financial measures. Reconciliation of these non-GAAP financial measures to the most directly comparable U.S. GAAP measures can be found in our earnings press release and our company's 8-K filing dated today, November 5th, 2026. We will also reference reported and organic operational growth. Organic operational growth excludes the effect of foreign currency, as well as acquisitions and divestitures, which individually impact Zoetis' growth by 1% or more.

Unless otherwise stated, all revenue growth performance metrics will be based on organic operational performance. With that, I will turn the call over to Kristin. Kristin?

Kristin Peck:Thank you, Mathieu. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Today, we reported our third quarter results with revenue and adjusted net income both declining in line with our expectations. Our diversified portfolio provided some resilience, and we focused on defending leadership positions with investments in key franchises. At the same time, we continued advancing the portfolio and innovation pipeline. While challenging dynamics are continuing, we are seeing progress in the actions we are taking and have narrowed our full-year revenue guidance to the high end of our range.

As I walk you through our performance, I want to put the industry and company results in perspective and outline how we are positioning Zoetis for the near and long term. But first, I am pleased to welcome Jay to his first earnings call with Zoetis. He brings a strong track record and a valuable combination of financial and operating experience, and we're excited to have him on the team. With that, let me start with what we see across the industry. As you all know, animal health remains a long-term secular growth industry, driven by a growing global population looking to eat more protein and adopt and care for more pets.

Like most industries, however, animal health is not immune to cyclical factors, which affect pet care and livestock differently. In developed pet care markets, veterinary service costs have risen 50% since 2022, well ahead of general inflation. Alongside softer consumer confidence, that cost pressure is making pet owners more value-conscious and deliberate when making trade-offs to care for their pets. The mix of pets is also changing. High housing costs are affecting homeownership and pet adoption, with fewer dogs joining households as cat ownership continues to grow. Because dogs are more medicalized than cats, this shift also affects underlying demand for veterinary services.

These pressures are reflected in the continued weakness in U.S. clinic visits, which are down 3% year to date across categories. These dynamics, combined with intense competition in key franchises, continue to weigh on our companion animal revenue this quarter. At the same time, the bond between people and their pets remains strong. In the U.S., the Human Animal Bond Research Institute's latest survey found that 98% of pet owners experience health benefits from their pets, and 91% said knowing about those benefits makes them more likely to maintain their pet's health. That enduring bond is an important foundation for our industry, but it exists alongside real barriers.

37% of people planning to get a pet cited the cost of ownership as a concern. As the industry leader, we are focused on meeting customers where they are. That means working with veterinary practices to support their profitability and success while developing programs to help pet owners manage the cost of care. In contrast, livestock is benefiting from growing demand for quality protein sources. We're also seeing growing demand on animal health to improve productivity, support food security, and adopt a One Health approach. That demand has contributed to historic industry growth, and for Zoetis, underscores the strength of a broad and diverse portfolio.

While we expect livestock to remain a strong contributor over the short, medium, and long term, disease, weather, and local production cycles will continue to influence year-to-year results. Diversity matters, not only across species, but across geographies. Growth conditions vary significantly from market to market, reflecting differences in economic and geopolitical conditions, species mix, and regulatory environment. In many developed markets, pet care represents a larger and more medicalized share of the animal health market, while in many emerging markets, livestock does. As a result, the same economic shifts can affect markets in very different ways. Tariffs and trade flows continue to evolve, and our commercial strategies reflect the conditions in each market.

That local focus matters because emerging markets are expected to remain the fastest-growing part of animal health, with room to bring more animals into regular care, gain share, and broaden access to innovation. Which brings me to what we're doing to defend and grow our leadership. Building on the actions we've outlined over the past two quarters, today, I'll focus on three priorities: leveraging the diversity of our portfolio, expanding access to established franchises, and advancing innovation. I'll take you through each with examples of how they're showing up across our key franchises. First, we're leveraging the advantage that comes from the diversity and differentiation of our portfolio.

Competition is increasingly playing out product by product, but our range of options within the therapeutic categories and across channels gives us more ways to meet customer needs and compete effectively. Those choices are especially important in our key dermatology franchise, where share pressure is most acute. We are continuing to sharpen commercial execution, directing resources where they can influence customer decisions, and reinforcing the value of our differentiated portfolio with vets and pet owners. For example, we're using that breadth to drive conversion to Apoquel Chew with chew in the room promotion and in-clinic sampling, highlighting a more convenient alternative that can support treatment compliance.

At the same time, we expect U.S. approval of long-acting Cytopoint in the fourth quarter, adding a more convenient option for chronic itch, a segment that accounts for more than 60% of global dermatology doses. We're using that added diversity to build awareness for the next option in derm, with a teaser campaign ahead of approval. Similarly, since the beginning of the year, we faced mounting generic competition for Convenia and Cerenia. We acted swiftly, and this quarter, we saw the pace of share gains moderate for the first time since entry.

With recent FDA approval in the U.S. and its coming launch in Canada, Convenia RTU for dogs extends the portfolio with a single injection that can provide up to 14 days of treatment. Second, we're expanding access to our established franchises and investing in the evidence and medical support that help vets navigate a more selective market. When visits are down and owners are weighing the cost of care, the clinical conversation matters. Veterinarians need to identify patients who can benefit and have relevant evidence to support treatment decisions. This is a central role of medical affairs, and one reason we launched the Medical Hub, which houses our scientific insights, publications, and educational materials in one place for veterinary teams.

That approach is relevant in parasiticides, where softer end market demand is creating pressure. Even with double-digit declines in U.S. flea, tick, and heartworm clinic visits, the Simparica franchise delivered modest growth this quarter, as expanded access to Simparica Trio drove growth internationally. Trio's triple combination protection gives vets a differentiated option, supported by recent peer-reviewed research on heartworm resistance. One example of scientific evidence supporting the franchise is a recent peer-reviewed speed of kill study available through the Medical Hub, and our continued investments in phase IV studies provides vets with relevant evidence in a more selective market.

We also now expect approval of Simparica Duo by year-end, ahead of our original timeline, broadening the portfolio and extending access to customers with unmet needs. This same strategy applies to OA pain. We're building the category, but it requires sustained effort to improve disease awareness and help veterinarians identify more patients who could benefit from treatment. We are clear-eyed about the work ahead and measured in our expectations. At the same time, just four years ago, alternatives to NSAIDs were limited. Today, our portfolio offers dogs and cats monthly or longer-acting three-month pain relief. Recent approvals and launches of Lenivia and Portela extend those options, and we believe broader access will build the category over time.

These are strong franchises in markets we help build. Our focus is to support customers through current pressures while continuing to invest in their growth. Third, we continue to advance innovation while remaining disciplined in how we allocate capital. In this environment, that means taking costs out where needed to operate more efficiently while protecting investments in innovation and advancing our robust pipeline. Lifecycle innovation is central to the first. The examples I have discussed in derm, paras, and OA pain strengthen established franchises and help create resilience in a pressured market. We are applying this same approach to livestock through new formulations and expanded indications across the portfolio, including FDA emergency use authorization of Dectomax for New World screwworm.

These extensions help keep our portfolio relevant to evolving customer needs and support franchise contribution over time. Last year, at our innovation webcast, we committed to achieving a significant major market approval every year for the next several years. To date, we have met our 2026 milestones, and in some areas, moved ahead of schedule. For example, Convenia RTU has now received approvals in two major markets, both earlier than planned. Beyond lifecycle innovation, we are working to create new categories in areas such as renal disease, oncology, cardiology, and obesity, where diagnosis is essential to identifying patients who may benefit from treatment. That makes diagnostics a strategic enabler of this pipeline.

Our investments are building the tools and capabilities to support that work. This quarter, companion animal diagnostics delivered double-digit revenue growth, reflecting increased utilization and contributions from the strategic acquisitions of VitalRADS and VPG. Our market leadership was built on innovation. Sustaining it means extending the franchises we have today while building the capabilities that will enable the future of animal health. Before I turn it over to Jay, I want to be clear that while the companion animal market remains soft in the quarter, Zoetis' targeted commercial execution has helped mitigate the macro and competitive pressures, and we will continue to adapt our approach as the market evolves.

We remain focused on disciplined resource allocation paired with investments to grow markets and share. At Zoetis, that means directing resources to defend our key franchises today while advancing innovation for the future to drive strong growth over time. We have the portfolio, science, and customer relationships to do just that. With that, I am pleased to hand it over to Jay.

Jay Saccaro:Thanks, Kristin. I am excited to be here for my first earnings call with Zoetis. While I am just a few months in, my conviction in this company has only grown. The product and organization are world-class, and the innovation pipeline spanning CKD, oncology, and next-generation lifecycle products represents a real catalyst for long-term value creation. My near-term focus is on understanding our business and operations in detail, ensuring our cost structure is as competitive as our portfolio, and working alongside Kristin and the team to navigate the current market environment with discipline and transparency.

As I deepen my understanding of the business, we will also be evaluating the financial metrics we share related to guidance, and we look forward to sharing an update with you on the fourth quarter call. With that, let's look at the quarter. We delivered revenue of $2.4 billion, declining 1% on both a reported and organic operational basis, in line with our expectations, driven by a 1% price decline and flat volume.

Our U.S. segment revenue was $1.2 billion, down 6%, driven by declines in companion animal from our key dermatology portfolio, as well as the impact of generics on certain brands, while our international segment was $1.1 billion, up 4%, with growth across livestock, parasiticides, and OA pain more than offsetting dermatology headwinds. We delivered adjusted EPS of $1.75 in the quarter, up 1%, driven by the lower share count due to our ongoing share repurchase activity. Adjusted gross margin was 71%, down 30 basis points on a reported basis. Foreign exchange had a favorable impact of 30 basis points.

On an operational basis, gross margin was down 60 basis points, driven by the impact of our strategic pricing initiatives, product mix, and certain inventory-related charges, partially offset by refunds related to prior tariff assessments. Adjusted operating expenses were $749 million, flat operationally, with both adjusted SG&A of $571 million and adjusted R&D of $174 million also flat, reflecting the continued benefit of our cost and productivity programs, including lower incentive compensation and professional services savings, partially offset by increased R&D investments in data and digital initiatives and our broader project portfolio. Adjusted net income was $720 million, down 7% on an organic operational basis.

You will see that our GAAP results also included $78 million of an impairment charge on previously acquired in-process research and development assets, resulting from updated estimates of development and commercial assumptions. Let's look more closely at the key drivers of our revenue performance this quarter, starting with companion animal, where globally we declined 5% on $1.6 billion in revenue, driven by an 8% decline in the U.S. and flat performance internationally. Within companion animal, our performance was driven by key dermatology, which declined 16% globally on $396 million in sales, reflecting competitive headwinds and pricing actions across both segments.

In the U.S., we declined 13% in the quarter on $266 million in revenue, driven by share loss in Apoquel, which was slowed by our promotional investments, partially offset by volume growth in the chewable formulation, which now represents roughly half of total Apoquel volume. Cytopoint sales also declined, reflecting canine visit declines of approximately 5% in the quarter, with pruritic visits specifically down 3%, as well as broader affordability pressures on pet owner spending. Direct competitive impact from new launches in the injectable dermatology space were minimal. Internationally, key dermatology was $130 million, down 20%, with pressure most acute in Europe, where new entrants drove volume losses across the Apoquel franchise.

Cytopoint proved more resilient, given its differentiation in international markets. In addition to declines in key dermatology, generic competition in Cerenia and Convenia continued to pressure U.S. results. While volume declines moderated to their lowest level since generics entered the market in Q1, we continue to manage through a challenging competitive dynamic. Partially offsetting these declines, our Simparica franchise grew 1% on global revenue of $358 million. The results were mixed across our segments. Internationally, we grew 10% on revenue of $99 million, driven by strong Simparica Trio momentum across Europe and Latin America, partially offset by expected erosion in Simparica as customers continue transitioning to the triple combination product.

In the U.S., the franchise declined 2% on $259 million in revenue, as accelerating declines in flea, tick, and heartworm clinic visits were partially offset by volume gains from our cross-portfolio promotion. Our OA pain meds generated $137 million in sales, increasing 2% globally. We continue to see contributions from the launch of Lenivia and Portela in the EU and Canada, which drove 13% growth internationally on $86 million in revenue, with both products gaining traction quickly and early satisfaction scores from veterinarians and pet owners remaining exceptionally high. Meanwhile, in the U.S., OA pain meds contributed $51 million in total, declining 12%.

Lower OA visits and ongoing safety perception headwinds weighed on Librela adoption and daily sales trends, partially offset by Solensia's resilience, supported by stable patient share and increased feline clinic visits in the quarter. Companion animal diagnostics delivered $122 million in revenue, up 13% globally, with double-digit growth in both the U.S. and internationally. Growth was driven primarily by recent acquisitions in both segments, including VitalRADS in the U.S. and VPG in the U.K. and Ireland, with continued underlying adoption of our point-of-care and Imagyst platforms contributing to the remainder. Innovation across the diagnostics portfolio continues to advance, with OptiCell gaining traction in hematology and OmniMax, our next-generation point-of-care analyzer, on the horizon.

Now, moving on to livestock, which delivered $797 million, up 7%, with contributions across both the U.S. and international. U.S. livestock grew 5% on $266 million in revenue, supported by reliable Ceftiofur supply driving cattle performance, broad-based swine growth, and strong poultry vaccine demand. Internationally, we saw sales of $531 million and growth of 9%, led by cattle strength across the segment and outstanding fish performance, driven by higher vaccination rates in Norway. Our capital allocation priorities remain unchanged. We will continue to invest in R&D and internal innovation, the engine of our long-term growth, while remaining disciplined in pursuing bolt-on business development opportunities.

After internal reinvestment and business development, excess capital is returned to shareholders, as demonstrated by the $2.4 billion distributed in 2026 through the third quarter in the form of both buybacks and dividends. Now, turning to our updated full-year guidance for 2026. Q3 delivered in line with our expectations, giving us the confidence to update our full-year guidance range. We are narrowing our full-year revenue guidance to $9.22 billion-$9.32 billion, representing an organic operational decline of -2% to -1% year over year. We are raising our adjusted net income guidance to $2.6 billion-$2.64 billion, representing organic operational decline of -7% to -5%. We are also raising adjusted diluted EPS to $6.25 to $6.35.

To close, our diverse portfolio and disciplined commercial execution continue to help us navigate an operating environment shaped by competitive pressure in our key companion animal franchises, softer clinic visits, and ongoing affordability headwinds for pet owners. But we are also seeing strength in livestock and solid momentum in diagnostics. Before I turn it over to the operator, I wanted to share a brief word on 2027. While it is too early to provide specific guidance, we will plan prudently for the upcoming year. We will not be assuming improvements in the macro environment or pet owner spending trends, and we expect the competitive dynamics we have mentioned to remain a factor throughout most of the year.

At the same time, we are encouraged by the commercial strategies we are executing, and most importantly, we are excited about the innovations planned for 2027 and 2028. While we expect limited revenue contribution from these launches in 2027, their impact should build later in the year and into 2028. We look forward to sharing more about this on our Q4 call. Our focus remains on executing with discipline and positioning the business for improved performance over time. With that, I will turn it over to the operator for questions. Operator?

Operator:Thank you. If you would like to ask a question at this time, please press star one on your telephone keypad. If at any point your question has been answered, you may remove yourself from the queue by pressing star two. In the interest of time, we ask that you limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. When posing your question, please pick up your handset to allow optimal sound quality. Our first question is coming from Chris Schott with JPMorgan. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Chris Schott:Thanks so much for the questions. I guess the first one for me would be great just to get additional color on the impact the promotional activities you initiated this year are having on the business. I guess specifically, I am just trying to get my hands around what areas do these seem to be gaining traction, and are there areas where you have not yet seen an impact? My second question was just maybe building on some of those 2027 comments that you just made. Just as you think about the various pushes and pulls, are just there any other considerations we should be keeping in mind for next year's numbers?

Trying to get my hands around directionally, do you see the street in the right place with both top line and EPS currently? Thanks so much.

Kristin Peck:Great. Thanks, Chris. I will take your first question. I will let Jay take your second. As we spoke about on our last few calls, our pricing strategy is really focused on retaining volume and gaining share, and it is really focused on deliberate, analytically supported actions that are protecting list price, but really focusing on gross-to-net investments. We were quite pleased with the performance of those investments in the quarter, specifically, and some of these facts are in our slides that we shared as well. The promotional defense on derm managed to slow U.S. dermatology share loss in the quarter to 4 points in Q3. It was about 7 points in Q2 overall in derm.

So, really pleased with really slowing that overall decline in share loss there. As you think about how they came through in our parasiticides, we are really pleased that we held share in the quarter with Simparica Trio at a 22.5% share, and we remain the market leader in puppies, which I think is a really important future prediction of sales there. So, we were very pleased. Again, we are going to stay focused and continue to watch the market as it evolves, and make sure we are targeting our investments to make sure we continue to protect share and ultimately grow it. Jay, do you want to take the second?

Jay Saccaro:Sure. So, look, we are in the middle of our budgeting process as we speak, so it is definitely too early to comment very specifically about 2027, but we did want to share some guiding principles. I think from our perspective, as we approach 2027, we are going to be conservative or prudent as we put together our numbers. We have seen some macro trends over the last several quarters. We are not going to assume a market change in macro factors.

We have seen some competitive dynamics, and while I think we walk away from the third quarter encouraged by the activity from a promotional and commercial standpoint, at the same time, we are not going to assume a change in competitive dynamic in 2027. Then, finally, as I come into the role here, one of the things I have spent a lot of time on is the R&D pipeline. It is incredibly exciting the work that our teams are doing, and the impact over time is going to be substantial. At the same time, it is not going to have a huge impact in 2027.

So, from our perspective, we are going to be very thoughtful as we put together our plan for 2027. I am hesitant to comment on street models or anything like that, certainly at this point. We are very excited about the long-term prospects that we have, but we are going to be clear-eyed as we approach 2027.

Operator:Thank you. Our next question comes from David Westenberg with Piper Sandler. Please go ahead.

David Westenberg:Thank you so much. We followed parasiticides for a while from topicals, the orals, isoxazoline. There has generally been a consistent pattern that a new product will come in, it will get some new generational starts, and then the market kind of matures and normalizes. We saw this when you launched Simparica. Originally, you did take share, but NexGard kind of settled in and kind of continued to grow. Is that what we think we could see in the 2027, 2028 market with Simparica, with some of the new entrants and new categories? What would make it different, and what kind of indicators would tell you that maybe growth would normalize in that category in 2027, 2028?

Again, I do not want to take away, you did grow 5% in Simparica Trio overall, but just curious on that, and I will have a follow-up.

Kristin Peck:Sure, Dave. I will take that first question before your follow-up. As I said, we were pleased with the performance of Simparica in the quarter. The franchise globally did about 1%. We did about 4% growth in Trio specifically. As I was just talking about, we are very pleased that in the U.S., we are the market leader and we maintained our share at 22.5%, which is almost two times our next biggest competitor. I also think it is important if you think about parasiticides, just like the U.S. from international, we are seeing significantly higher growth in international overall. I think you are seeing this because triple combination category is still in its infancy there.

We are really expanding and entering new markets, so we see Trio is still early in its penetration, and we believe there is really a long runway for growth there. We are continuing to invest in innovation in this space. As we also mentioned, we are expecting approval of Simparica Duo by year end, which is ahead of its original timeline. I think this will continue to broaden our portfolio. I guess the way we see the market, we think there is still significant opportunity to continue to expand this market from single combinations, from topicals and collars, into triple combination, as well as to gain share.

We have a very comprehensive portfolio that we think is differentiated, and we will continue to invest there. I will maybe move to your second question.

David Westenberg:Sure. Cytopoint, as you noted, has held in well. There isn't anything in the market like it right now. Befrena does have a label of four to eight weeks efficacy, looks pretty competitive as it launches in 2027. Can you walk us through both first, maybe from a defensive strategy perspective early on, and then maybe from an offensive strategy as you get your own long-acting product? Can you confirm that long-acting is still on time? I think you said Q4, you do expect approval. How fast is that to roll out? Thank you so much for taking the questions.

Kristin Peck:Sure. Thanks. We continue to believe that Cytopoint and the long-acting space in derm is really exciting. As we mentioned, it did fare better in the quarter. I think that's really because the customers are on it are quite pleased with the efficacy of the product overall. As you know, we did have a new entrant in that category in the U.S. To date, they've had limited share given their supply challenges. What we are really excited about as we see in this category is to continue to expand it. We are expecting the approval of Cytopoint long-acting this year. We think Cytopoint will help us expand the category, honestly.

It provides a more convenient option that lasts longer, which is really helpful for busy pet owners who coming in every month might be a challenge. This is part of the Zoetis strategy to continue to innovate in each of our key therapeutic areas to both make sure that we can continue to grow our share, as well as expand the market overall. We're pleased to have that product, and we look forward to launching it in the first half of next year. We are on track with Cytopoint long-acting, and we think it'll be a great addition to continue to build this brand.

Operator:Thank you. We will move next with Jon Block with Stifel. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Jon Block:Great. Thanks, guys. Good morning. Jay, I am arriving at an implied 4Q 2026 organic revenue growth rate of around -3%, off an easy comp. Maybe just your thoughts on that, if accurate, any color. Then maybe more importantly, what does this mean for the business looking forward? If you could give us some color there, then I will ask the follow-up.

Jay Saccaro:Sure. I think as we think about the fourth quarter, it really is important to take it in the context of the third and fourth quarter and also the full year. On the first half, we were down about 1 point. The third quarter was down a bit more than that. As we look at the third and fourth quarter together, we are talking about a full year growth rate leading to a decline of -1% to -2%. We historically see some seasonality with higher sales in the third quarter and then the fourth quarter.

In this particular case, with the promotional activity that we pursued in the third quarter, we are anticipating a third to fourth quarter decline in the high single-digit range. Very much in line with our expectations, although I would say the market and our performance has been a little bit better than our anticipation. Related to that, we always anticipated a deceleration in the fourth quarter versus the third. As we think about what this means for the overall health of the business, it really is important to consider it in the context of the third quarter as well.

Jon Block:Okay, that is helpful. Thank you. Then, I guess just to pivot, livestock continues to be the bright spot, pardon me, for you guys. You might exit 2026, or pardon me, 2026 might have a comp of high single digits. Maybe if you could just give us some thoughts on sustainability of livestock. Kristin, you mentioned the protein tailwinds, and that does not look like it is going away anytime soon. But just looking forward for this business off a high single-digit comp that might add some screwworm tailwinds in there, how do we think about that for 2027 and beyond? Thank you.

Kristin Peck:Yeah. We were quite pleased with the performance of livestock in the quarter. It grew 7% overall, and really underlying that, as you mentioned, is demand for quality protein, and that's really across the globe, I would say. We saw U.S. delivering 5% to the quarter and international at 9% in the quarter. If you think about that, international livestock is a higher percentage of our business, as we've talked about, and that growth was really broad overall across species. We are confident that livestock will remain a strong contributor. Obviously, as we see, there's definitely a little more cyclicality historically in livestock. It's influenced by disease, by weather, by outbreaks, local production cycles overall.

But there were a few years, obviously, as you recall, where Zoetis had an LOE, and we also had African swine fever outbreaks. Historically, livestock is a solid contributor overall as an industry grower, and specifically for Zoetis, we're quite focused in our portfolio, as we've mentioned, around vaccines and genetics and preventatives, which we think has positioned us well as we see strong continued demand for protein.

Operator:Thank you. We will move next with Brandon Vazquez with William Blair. Please go ahead.

Brandon Vazquez:Hey, good morning. Thanks for taking the questions. Kristin, I wanted to follow up on your commentary about you guys have been pretty successful, it seems like, in defending share in some of the gross-to-net promotional activities, maybe for lack of a better phrase to use there. The question being, do you think that these gross-to-net promotional activities are short-term in nature? Is this something you're doing to combat kind of temporary entrants from competitors, or do you think on a go-forward basis that you'll need to keep this new gross-to-net? Part of the question is basically, what are the implications to your margins and your gross margins on a go-forward basis within the companion animal business?

Kristin Peck:Yeah, I mean, it's a great question. I think our focus right now is with a lot of new entrants in both derm and parasiticides. Historically, as you know, in our space, when new entrants came, they expanded the market. We aren't seeing that right now, and so we've had to be a little more focused on some of these gross-to-net investments. Ultimately, we think when share settles out, and historically you've seen that somewhere between 12 and 18 months, and what we're really watching for to know how to tweak, and we're constantly watching every month, but certainly every quarter, is how are we seeing those shares stabilize?

When we see two quarters where those shares pretty much stayed, we'll have a sense that those shares have stabilized, and we can then really focus more on gaining share and growing the market overall. I don't think these are here forever, but I think as Jay mentioned in his remarks, I think some of these new products have only recently entered in certain markets, and this is a market-specific investment. We think we need to lap those new entrants for both derm and paras to really have a sense of how to continue to adjust our gross-to-net investments.

But I think our strategy, as I mentioned earlier, is making sure at the very least we defend our share, and we're focused on both growing share and growing these markets ultimately. The reality is there are still way more untreated animals in both of these categories than there are treated animals. Cytopoint sales also declined, reflecting canine visit declines of approximately 5% in the quarter, with pruritic visits specifically down 3%, as well as broader affordability pressures on pet owner spending. Direct competitive impact from new launches in the injectable dermatology space were minimal. Internationally, key dermatology was $130 million, down 20%, with pressure most acute in Europe, where new entrants drove volume losses across the Apoquel franchise.

Cytopoint proved more resilient, given its differentiation in international markets. In addition to declines in key dermatology, generic competition in Cerenia and Convenia continued to pressure U.S. results. While volume declines moderated to their lowest level since generics entered the market in Q1, we continue to manage through a challenging competitive dynamic. Partially offsetting these declines, our Simparica franchise grew 1% on global revenue of $358 million. The results were mixed across our segments. Internationally, we grew 10% on revenue of $99 million, driven by strong Simparica Trio momentum across Europe and Latin America, partially offset by expected erosion in Simparica as customers continue transitioning to the triple combination product.

In the U.S., the franchise declined 2% on $259 million in revenue, as accelerating declines in flea, tick, and heartworm clinic visits were partially offset by volume gains from our cross-portfolio promotion. Our OA pain meds generated $137 million in sales, increasing 2% globally. We continue to see contributions from the launch of Lenivia and Portela in the EU and Canada, which drove 13% growth internationally on $86 million in revenue, with both products gaining traction quickly and early satisfaction scores from veterinarians and pet owners remaining exceptionally high. Meanwhile, in the U.S., OA pain meds contributed $51 million in total, declining 12%.

Lower OA visits and ongoing safety perception headwinds weighed on Librela adoption and daily sales trends, partially offset by Solensia's resilience, supported by stable patient share and increased feline clinic visits in the quarter. Companion animal diagnostics delivered $122 million in revenue, up 13% globally, with double-digit growth in both the U.S. and internationally. Growth was driven primarily by recent acquisitions in both segments, including VitalRADS in the U.S. and VPG in the U.K. and Ireland, with continued underlying adoption of our point-of-care and Imagyst platforms contributing to the remainder. Internationally, we saw sales of $531 million and growth of 9%, led by cattle strength across the segment and outstanding fish performance, driven by higher vaccination rates in Norway. Our capital allocation priorities remain unchanged. We will continue to invest in R&D and internal innovation, the engine of our long-term growth, while remaining disciplined in pursuing bolt-on business development opportunities.

We are raising our adjusted net income guidance to $2.6 billion-$2.64 billion, representing organic operational decline of -7% to -5%. We are also raising adjusted diluted EPS to $6.25 to $6.35.

To close, our diverse portfolio and disciplined commercial execution continue to help us navigate an operating environment shaped by competitive pressure in our key companion animal franchises, softer clinic visits, and ongoing affordability headwinds for pet owners.
